html:
A barrel-shaped clay cylinder covered in Akkadian cuneiform, written in the name of Cyrus the Great after he took Babylon in 539 BCE. It was buried in the foundations of the city wall, as Mesopotamian kings had long done with building records.

The text condemns the last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, as an impious ruler and says the god Marduk chose Cyrus to set things right. It describes a peaceful entry into the city, then says Cyrus restored temples, returned the statues of gods to their shrines and let deported peoples go home. It does not name the Jews, but it fits the Bible's account of the Return to Zion.

The cylinder was dug up in Babylon in 1879 and is in the British Museum. In 1971 the Shah of Iran hailed it as the first charter of human rights, and a copy stands at the United Nations. Historians see it more as royal propaganda in an old Babylonian style, though the policy of restoring local worship was real.
